meta.title: Inventory management, just-in-time and backflush costing
meta.summary: The costs of holding inventory, the economic order quantity, reorder points and safety stock, the cost of prediction errors, just-in-time purchasing and production, and backflush costing.

videos.title: What inventory really costs
videos.take: Inventory costs include purchasing, ordering, carrying, stockout, quality and shrinkage costs

scenes.say: Inventory looks like an asset on the balance sheet. But holding it costs money every day.

scenes.heading: Six inventory costs
items: Carrying: storage, insurance, capital tied up
Quality: defects hidden in big batches
scenes.say: Six costs. Purchasing costs, the price. Ordering costs: preparing orders, freight and receiving. Carrying costs: storage, insurance and the return on the capital tied up. Stockout costs: lost sales and rush orders. Quality costs: defects hidden in big batches. And shrinkage: theft, damage and obsolescence.

sub: The return given up by tying
scenes.say: The biggest carrying cost is often invisible in the accounts: the opportunity cost of the capital tied up. Cash sitting in battery packs could be earning a return elsewhere.

scenes.heading: Carrying one battery pack for a year
scenes.say: A battery pack costs $310. At Tallgrass's eight percent cost of capital, holding one for a year costs $24.80, plus $2.20 of climate-controlled storage and insurance: twenty-seven dollars a year.

sub: Order often: low carrying, high ordering
scenes.say: The core trade-off: ordering often keeps carrying costs low but multiplies ordering costs. Ordering rarely does the reverse. The economic order quantity balances them.

opts: Return forgone on cash tied up in stock
scenes.say: Quick check. Which is a carrying cost? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, the opportunity cost of capital tied up in inventory.

videos.title: The economic order quantity
videos.take: EOQ = √(2DP ÷ C) balances ordering and carrying costs

scenes.say: How many battery packs should Tallgrass order at a time? The economic order quantity gives the answer.

sub: D: annual demand   P: cost per order
C: carrying cost per unit per year
scenes.say: The economic order quantity is the square root of two times annual demand times the cost per order, divided by the annual carrying cost per unit.

scenes.heading: Battery packs
scenes.say: Tallgrass uses twelve hundred packs a year. Each order costs a hundred eighty dollars to place and receive. Carrying a pack costs twenty-seven dollars a year. The EOQ is the square root of sixteen thousand: about a hundred twenty-six packs.

scenes.heading: Relevant costs at EOQ
scenes.say: At that quantity, Tallgrass places about nine and a half orders a year, costing about $1,700, and carries an average of sixty-three packs, also about $1,700. At the EOQ, ordering and carrying costs are equal.
The purchase price doesn't affect the EOQ, unless bigger orders earn quantity discounts, which must then be weighed against extra carrying costs.
Quick check. Annual demand two thousand, cost per order a hundred dollars, carrying cost ten dollars. What's the EOQ? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's A. The square root of forty thousand is two hundred.

videos.title: Reorder point and safety stock
videos.take: Reorder point = usage during lead time + safety stock

scenes.say: EOQ says how much to order. The reorder point says when.

sub: Usage per week × lead time in weeks
scenes.say: The reorder point is the inventory level at which to place a new order: expected usage during the lead time, plus any safety stock.

scenes.heading: Battery packs from overseas
scenes.say: Tallgrass uses about twenty-four packs a week, and overseas orders take eight weeks to arrive. That's a hundred ninety-two packs used while waiting. Add two weeks of safety stock, forty-eight packs, and the reorder point is two hundred forty.
Safety stock is a buffer against uncertainty: demand spikes in spring, or shipping delays at the ports.
How much safety stock? Enough that the expected cost of stockouts, lost sales and idle assembly lines, balances the extra carrying cost. For a key part like batteries, Tallgrass holds more.

scenes.q: Usage 30 a week; lead time 4 weeks; safety stock 40. Reorder point?
scenes.say: Quick check. Usage thirty a week, lead time four weeks, safety stock forty. Reorder point? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. A hundred twenty plus forty is a hundred sixty.

videos.title: The cost of a prediction error
videos.take: EOQ is robust to estimation errors; evaluation systems must reward managers for the right inventory decisions

scenes.say: Ana's estimates of ordering and carrying costs could be wrong. How much would a mistake cost?

scenes.heading: Actual ordering cost turns out to be $240
scenes.say: Suppose the true cost per order is $240, not $180. The true EOQ is a hundred forty-six packs, with relevant costs of $3,944. Ordering a hundred twenty-six, as Ana did, costs $3,987. The prediction error costs only forty-three dollars.

sub: Total cost is flat near the optimum
scenes.say: The EOQ model is robust: total cost is flat near the optimum, so moderate errors in the inputs cost little.

sub: If managers aren't charged for capital,
scenes.say: The bigger risk is behavioral. If the purchasing manager's performance ignores the cost of capital tied up in inventory, she has every reason to over-order and never run out.
The fix: charge managers for the capital their inventory ties up, so the decision model and the evaluation model agree.

scenes.q: A purchasing manager is judged only on purchase price variances and stockouts. What's the likely behavior?
opts: Order large batches to get discounts and avoid stockouts
scenes.say: Quick check. A purchasing manager is judged only on price variances and stockouts. What's the likely behavior? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B: big batches, ignoring the carrying costs she isn't charged for.

videos.title: Just-in-time purchasing and production
videos.take: JIT buys and makes only what's needed, when needed; it cuts carrying costs but demands reliable suppliers and quality

scenes.say: Just-in-time aims to hold almost no inventory: buy and make only what's needed, when it's needed.

scenes.heading: JIT production features
items: Cells that build a product start to finish
Total quality: defects stop the line
scenes.say: JIT production is pulled by actual demand rather than pushed by forecasts. Work is organized in cells that build a product from start to finish, with multi-skilled workers. Defects stop the line, because there's no inventory to hide behind. And fast setups make small batches economical.

scenes.heading: JIT frames from a supplier in Worthington
scenes.say: Tallgrass is considering daily frame deliveries from a supplier in nearby Worthington. Lower inventory saves $4,500 of carrying cost. Extra deliveries cost $3,200, and the expected cost of occasional stockouts is $600. The net benefit is $700, small but positive, plus floor space freed.
JIT suits local, reliable suppliers. Battery packs shipped from overseas with eight-week lead times aren't candidates, as supply-chain disruptions in recent years showed.
With little inventory, there's less need to track costs through work in process. That opens the door to simpler costing: backflush costing.

scenes.q: Which supplier is the best JIT candidate?
opts: Local frame maker, daily deliveries, 99% on time
Any supplier with the lowest price
A supplier with frequent quality problems
scenes.say: Quick check. Which supplier is the best JIT candidate? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B: local, frequent and reliable.

videos.title: Backflush costing
videos.take: Backflush costing skips recording work in process and assigns standard costs at a later trigger point

scenes.say: In a JIT plant, tracking every cost through work in process isn't worth the effort. Backflush costing takes a shortcut.

sub: costs assigned at trigger points using standards
scenes.say: Backflush costing omits some or all of the entries for the flow of costs through production. Costs are assigned to output using standard costs, at chosen trigger points, such as when materials are bought or when bikes are finished.

scenes.heading: Trigger: materials purchased
scenes.say: At Tallgrass's JIT assembly cell, the first trigger is buying materials: $112,200 for a hundred two bikes' worth of kits, debited to a combined materials and in-process inventory account.

scenes.heading: Trigger: 100 bikes finished
scenes.say: Conversion costs incurred are collected in a control account. When a hundred bikes are finished, the second trigger, their standard costs are backflushed: $1,100 of materials and $200 of conversion each. Debit finished goods $130,000.

Backflush is simple and cheap, and accurate when inventories are small and stable. If work in process is large or changes a lot, it misstates inventory and income, and it leaves less of an audit trail.

scenes.q: When is backflush costing least appropriate?
scenes.say: Quick check. When is backflush costing least appropriate? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B: large, fluctuating work in process.

warmup: Do you buy groceries once a week or every day? What does each approach cost you?
Weekly: fewer trips (ordering cost) but more food in the fridge (carrying, spoilage). Daily: the reverse. That's the EOQ trade-off.

case: In 2027, port delays stretched battery lead times from 8 to 14 weeks. Tallgrass ran out of packs for 3 weeks in April, losing 60 bike sales (CM $900 each). The purchasing manager, evaluated on purchase price variance, had been ordering 400 packs at a time for a 5% quantity discount. The CFO now proposes holding 6 weeks of safety stock.
Compute the stockout cost in April.
Compute the new reorder point with 14-week lead times and 6 weeks of safety stock.

How would you change the purchasing manager's evaluation?

Stockout: 60 × 900 = $54,000. Reorder point: 24 × 14 + 144 = 480 packs. Extra 4 weeks of safety stock (96 packs) × $27 = $2,592 a year: worth it. Evaluate purchasing on total inventory costs, including carrying and stockouts, not just price variances.
exam: Describe the costs associated with inventory and explain the EOQ trade-off.
Purchasing, ordering, carrying (including opportunity cost of capital), stockout, quality, shrinkage. EOQ balances ordering (falls with larger orders) and carrying (rises with larger orders).
D = 9,000 units, P = $250 an order, C = $5 a unit per year. Compute EOQ, orders per year and total relevant cost. Usage 180 a week, lead time 2 weeks, safety stock 100: reorder point?
